question: What are the main HTTP methods and what is each used for?
title: HTTP Methods Overview
direct_answer: The main HTTP methods are GET (read), POST (create), PUT (full update), PATCH (partial update), and DELETE (remove). Each maps to a CRUD operation and has specific safety and idempotency characteristics.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic REST knowledge and ability to map HTTP methods to operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying POST is for all writes or confusing PUT vs PATCH
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain idempotency for each method and the safe vs unsafe distinction

sections.title: HTTP Method Semantics
sections.content: HTTP methods define the intended operation on a resource. REST uses these standardized verbs so that API consumers know what to expect. The method choice affects caching, idempotency, and how intermediaries (proxies, browsers) handle requests.

sections.title: Methods and Their Uses
content: GET: Read resource — safe and idempotent, can be cached
POST: Create resource — not idempotent (calling twice creates two records)
PUT: Full update — idempotent (calling multiple times has same effect)
PATCH: Partial update — idempotent in practice, updates only specified fields
DELETE: Remove resource — idempotent (deleting twice returns 404, same end state)
HEAD: Like GET but returns only headers — used to check resource existence
OPTIONS: Returns allowed methods — used in CORS preflight

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The five main HTTP methods map to CRUD operations. GET reads data and is safe — no side effects. POST creates resources and isn't idempotent, so calling it twice creates two records. PUT does a full replacement — if you PUT with only some fields, the missing ones get nulled. PATCH is for partial updates, sending only the changed fields. DELETE removes the resource. A key distinction: GET and HEAD are safe methods because they don't modify state. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — calling them multiple times produces the same result.

question: What is idempotency and which HTTP methods are idempotent?
title: Idempotency in HTTP Methods
direct_answer: Idempotency means making the same request multiple times produces the same result. GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are idempotent. POST is not — calling POST twice may create two resources.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of REST semantics beyond just knowing which method does what
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying PATCH is not idempotent — it is idempotent if implemented correctly
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why idempotency matters for retry logic in distributed systems

sections.title: Why Idempotency Matters
sections.content: Idempotency is critical for reliability. In distributed systems, network failures may cause requests to be retried. If a DELETE request is retried, the resource is already gone — that's fine, same end state. If a POST is retried, you might create a duplicate order or payment — that's a serious problem.

sections.title: Idempotency by Method
content: Idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, PATCH (when implemented correctly)
Not idempotent: POST (each call creates a new resource)
Safe (no side effects): GET, HEAD
POST idempotency workaround: Idempotency-Key header (used in payment APIs)
PUT idempotency: sending PUT /users/1 {name: 'John'} 100 times always results in {name: 'John'}
DELETE idempotency: first call returns 200, subsequent calls return 404, but end state is same — resource is gone

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Idempotent means you can make the same request many times and the outcome is the same as making it once. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — deleting a user twice still leaves no user. POST is not idempotent — submitting an order form twice could charge the customer twice. This matters for retry logic: if a network request fails and you don't know if the server received it, it's safe to retry GET or DELETE but dangerous to retry POST without an idempotency key. Payment APIs like Stripe use Idempotency-Key headers to make POST safe to retry.

followup_questions: How does Stripe handle POST idempotency?
What happens when you retry a DELETE and the resource is already gone?

question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
title: PUT vs PATCH
direct_answer: PUT replaces the entire resource — missing fields become null. PATCH updates only the specified fields, leaving others unchanged. Use PATCH for partial updates to avoid accidentally nulling out fields.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the practical difference and when to use each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using PUT for partial updates, accidentally clearing fields
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JSON Patch (RFC 6902) for complex PATCH operations

sections.title: PUT vs PATCH Semantics
sections.content: PUT is a full replacement. If you have a user with {name: 'John', email: 'john@gmail.com', age: 30} and you PUT {name: 'Johnny'}, the result is {name: 'Johnny', email: null, age: null}. PATCH sends only what changed: PATCH {name: 'Johnny'} gives {name: 'Johnny', email: 'john@gmail.com', age: 30}.

sections.title: Key Differences
content: PUT: full replacement — client sends complete representation
PATCH: partial update — client sends only changed fields
PUT requires client to know entire current state
PATCH is more efficient — smaller request payloads
In Spring Boot: @PutMapping vs @PatchMapping
JSON Patch (RFC 6902): structured format for PATCH operations [{op: 'replace', path: '/name', value: 'Johnny'}]

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The difference is scope. PUT replaces the entire resource — if you don't include a field, it gets cleared. PATCH only updates what you send. In practice, most APIs use PATCH for updates because it's safer and more efficient. You only send what changed. In Spring Boot, you use @PatchMapping annotation. One thing to watch out for: PATCH requests in Spring Boot can be tricky because request body binding will set fields to null if not provided — you often need to merge the existing entity with the patch manually.

followup_questions: How do you implement PATCH in Spring Boot without nulling other fields?
When would you still prefer PUT over PATCH?

question: What are safe HTTP methods and why does the distinction matter?
title: Safe HTTP Methods
direct_answer: Safe methods are those that don't modify server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. They can be called repeatedly without side effects. Browsers and proxies may freely cache or prefetch safe requests without concern.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the contract between HTTP methods and intermediaries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing safe with idempotent — all safe methods are idempotent but not vice versa
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how browsers use the safe/unsafe distinction (e.g., not preloading DELETE links)

sections.title: What Makes a Method Safe?
sections.content: A method is safe if it doesn't change resource state. GET /users/1 just reads — no change. DELETE /users/1 removes — not safe. This distinction matters because browsers and crawlers know they can follow GET links freely. If a GET link triggered a delete, that would be catastrophic (and is why CSRF attacks target state-changing methods).

sections.title: Safe vs Idempotent
content: Safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — read-only, no state change
All safe methods are also idempotent
Idempotent but not safe: PUT, DELETE — change state but same result if repeated
Not safe, not idempotent: POST — changes state and not safe to repeat
Browser prefetch: only prefetches safe URLs
CSRF tokens: only needed for unsafe methods that change state

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Safe methods — GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — don't change server state. Browsers exploit this: they can preload pages linked with GET without worrying about side effects. All safe methods are also idempotent, but the reverse isn't true. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe — they change state, just predictably. POST is neither safe nor idempotent. This distinction matters for things like CSRF protection — you only need CSRF tokens for unsafe methods like POST, PUT, and DELETE.

followup_questions: Why are CSRF attacks typically against POST not GET?
Can GET requests have side effects in practice?
What is the OPTIONS method used for?

question: How do you map HTTP methods to Spring Boot controller annotations?
title: HTTP Methods in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Spring Boot provides @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, and @DeleteMapping annotations that map HTTP methods to controller methods. These are shortcuts for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET) etc.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring Boot knowledge alongside HTTP theory
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @PostMapping for updates or not knowing that @GetMapping can't have a request body
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show proper ResponseEntity usage and mention @PathVariable vs @RequestParam

sections.title: Spring Boot Method Annotations
sections.content: Spring Boot makes it easy to implement HTTP methods with dedicated annotations. Each annotation maps to the corresponding HTTP verb and handles request deserialization and response serialization automatically when combined with @RestController.

sections.title: Annotations and Usage
content: @GetMapping("/users/{id}") — read, use @PathVariable Long id
@PostMapping("/users") — create, use @RequestBody UserRequest body, return 201 Created
@PutMapping("/users/{id}") — full update, @RequestBody UserRequest body
@PatchMapping("/users/{id}") — partial update, merge with existing entity
@DeleteMapping("/users/{id}") — delete, return 204 No Content
Return ResponseEntity<> for full control over status code and headers
@RequestParam for query params: /users?page=0&size=10

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: In Spring Boot, each HTTP method has a corresponding annotation. @GetMapping for reads, @PostMapping for creates, @PutMapping for full updates, @PatchMapping for partial updates, and @DeleteMapping for deletes. I typically use ResponseEntity as the return type to explicitly control the status code — returning 201 Created after POST, 204 No Content after DELETE. For path parameters like /users/123, I use @PathVariable. For query strings like /users?role=admin, I use @RequestParam. These annotations are just shortcuts for @RequestMapping with a method parameter.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
When should you return ResponseEntity vs just the object?
